source.title: What Causes Polysemanticity? An Alternative Origin Story of Mixed Selectivity from Incidental Causes
source.authors: Victor Lecomte; Kushal Thaman; Rylan Schaeffer; Naomi Bashkansky; Trevor Chow; Sanmi Koyejo

record.tranche_reason: The paper argues that polysemanticity can arise incidentally from regularization even when there are enough neurons to represent features separately, and reports toy-network results on the number of polysemantic neurons.
record.gate_note: The reported count of polysemantic neurons in the l1-regularized autoencoder bears on V4's regularization-cause component. The paper does not test interpretability shares in language models or vision models, attribution graphs, explanation accuracy, or the essay's tools and architecture comparisons. Results in Figures 4–6 primarily report sparsity proxies or a specific weight configuration, not a separately measured polysemantic-neuron count; they are not recorded as rows. Results cited from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: In a toy autoencoder with enough neurons (m ≥ n), the study counts polysemantic neurons produced by l1 regularization. That bears only on V4's causal component: messy neurons can come from regularization rather than lack of capacity. It does not measure interpretable-neuron shares in real models, tools or architectures.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add two points. The authors argue incidental polysemanticity can persist until neurons roughly equal features squared. They suggest it could be reduced by nudging training dynamics, for example neuron duplication, without changing the architecture.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a shallow, tied-weight nonlinear autoencoder trained on basis-vector inputs and counts polysemantic neurons; it does not perform a neuron-pole explanation audit or test explanations on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: The count varies with hidden-layer size m; the paper reports a Θ(n²/m) trend.
record.problems: Evidence is from a deliberately simplified toy autoencoder, not a modern language or vision model. Figure 3 is summarized by a trend and approximate constant rather than per-run values, and no uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 4–6 report sparsity proxies under noise or regularization and a specific weight configuration, rather than a separately measured polysemantic-neuron count relevant to the tested version.

untested.parts: Late-layer neurons in real vision or language models; weak explanation tools; modern architectures; the share of interpretable neurons rising with better tools or architecture; the ~5% to ~99% estimates for InceptionV1-sized models.
All of it: the Qwen3-32B pole audit and its shares.
All of it: shares across other models, dense and mixture-of-experts, and scale.
All of it: the InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose, and recursive generalization.
All of it: neuron attribution graphs and reconstruction error.
All of it: whether explanations fitted to activating examples predict activations.
All of it: simulation-based automated scoring.

missing.what: Neural-noise route: bipolar (negative-kurtosis) noise pushes encodings toward sparsity while normal noise does not. Figure 6 shows one encoding left spread across 7 neurons, a noise-induced polysemantic configuration. This is reported only via fourth-norm proxies and one example, with no polysemantic-neuron count.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence is purely from a toy model, and the link to V4 is indirect. The paper studies the causes of polysemanticity, not interpretable-neuron shares or tools. The polysemanticity here is genuine mixing of unrelated features, not a misreading. No uncertainty estimates are reported for Figure 3.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B pole audit and the stated shares of one-job, two-related-job, and not-understood poles.
Similar shares across language models, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, or models up to trillions of parameters.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, shared pose feature, and recursive generalization.

The study tests whether regularization can produce polysemanticity in a toy autoencoder. It does not test late-layer neurons, weak explanation tools, modern architectures, changes in interpretable-neuron share with tools or architecture, or the estimates for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Attribution graphs using a large model's own neurons and reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fitted to activating examples fail to predict activation on new inputs.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations on new text.

rows.subject: non-linear autoencoder
rows.size_stated: n ≈ 256 features; hidden layer m ranged from 256 to 4096 neurons
rows.operation_detail: Counted polysemantic neurons after training an l1-regularized nonlinear autoencoder.

conditions.value: used; parameter value not stated for these runs

rows.value: Experiments show a Θ(n²/m) trend; the stated constant 1/4 seems fairly accurate.
rows.note: The paper reports the trend across 16 training runs and the stated m range, rather than individual run values in the prose. It presents this as incidental polysemanticity despite m ≥ n.
rows.check: The baseline should be stated. A capacity-only account predicts zero polysemantic neurons, since m ≥ n. The theory predicts about n²/(4m) polysemantic neurons, and Figure 3 matches that prediction across 16 runs. The subject is a tied-weight toy autoencoder trained on basis vectors, not a vision or language model, so the row bears only on V4's regularization-not-capacity cause.

relationships.condition: Toy tied-weight ReLU autoencoder with l1 regularization, n=256, m from 256 to 4096
relationships.reason: r1: polysemantic neurons appear despite m ≥ n, following about n²/(4m). This supports regularization rather than capacity as a cause, in a toy setting only.
relationships.display_finding: Polysemantic neurons appeared even with at least as many neurons (m) as features (n), their number following about n²/(4m), which points to regularization rather than capacity as a cause in this toy setting.

source_check.reason: r1: polysemantic neurons appear with m ≥ n and follow about n²/(4m). This shows a non-capacity cause (l1 plus random initialization), in a toy setting only.

relationships.reason: r1 and Section 5: incidental polysemanticity persists until neurons roughly equal features squared, and is driven by random initialization. Removing the regularization cause is therefore not simply a matter of adding neurons.

source_check.reason: The label fits on r1's width effect. The polysemantic count falls as about n²/(4m) from m=256 to 4096, so width still sets how many messy neurons there are even with surplus neurons. This qualifies 'not capacity'. The record's reason ('not simply a matter of adding neurons') agrees with V4 and should be restated around this width dependence.

tranche.reason: A different method (toy autoencoder theory and experiments, no neuron-explanation audit) aimed at the same question: whether messy neurons come from lack of capacity or from other factors such as regularization.

source_check.notes: Toy only: one-hot basis inputs, tied weights, n ≈ 256. The Θ(n²/m) fit is shown only in Figure 3 (no numbers in the text), and λ for those runs is not stated. Section 3 also shows incidental polysemanticity from bipolar hidden-layer noise with no l1 term. No row records this, and it would bear on V4's 'regularization' cause.

statements.problem: The numbers for this study are right: tied weights, ReLU output, l1, n ≈ 256, m from 256 to 4096, 16 runs (Fig. 3) and about n²/(4m). Section 2.1 assumes m ≥ n. Preprint, no code.

statements.correction: Toy tied-weight l1 autoencoder, n ≈ 256: polysemantic neurons appear despite m ≥ n. Their count follows about n²/(4m) as m rises from 256 to 4096, so it falls with width but persists until m ≈ n². Cause: random initialization plus training dynamics under l1. Study's V4 verdicts are supports and limits_scope, not challenges.
statements.problem: The sentence is accurate: Section 5 says it can persist until neurons roughly equal features squared, contingent on random initialization and training dynamics. But under 'Capacity changes neuron interpretability' in a challenges block, it hides that the study's main result is polysemanticity despite m ≥ n (supports 'not capacity'). It also leaves out the width effect itself. The study has no challenges verdict.
What it says about this study is right: in the l1-regularized toy autoencoder, incidental polysemanticity arises.
Right: Section 2.5 reports the polysemantic count follows Θ(n²/m) as hidden size m varies, with constant about 1/4.
Makes no specific claim about this study and cites no rows from it.
